tool.name: Make
tool.tagline: Rebuild only what changed: the classic dependency-driven build tool
tool.description: Make reads a Makefile of rules saying how each file is built from others and reruns only the steps whose inputs changed. It builds C and C++ projects, and many teams also use it as a simple, universal task runner for tests, linting and deploys.

glossary.def: The text file of rules that make reads: which files are made from which, and the commands that make them.
In make, the thing a rule produces, usually a file name such as app or main.o, or a task name such as test.
In make, a file or target that a target is made from; it must be up to date before the target's recipe runs.
In make, the tab-indented shell commands under a rule that create or update its target.
The target make builds when you run plain make: the first target in the Makefile unless set otherwise.
A half-finished piece of a program (usually a .o file) made by compiling one source file; the linker joins object files into the finished program.
In C and C++, a small file (.h) of shared declarations that source files pull in with #include.
A make target that names a task, not a file (like clean or test), declared with .PHONY so it always runs.
A tool that gives a project a menu of named commands, such as make test or make run, so everyone runs tasks the same way.
A make variable set with =: any $(...) inside it is filled in again each time the variable is used.
A make variable set with :=: its value is worked out once, when it's defined.
A variable make sets inside each recipe, such as $@ (the target), $< (the first prerequisite) and $^ (all prerequisites).
A make rule with % in it, such as %.o: %.c, that works for every file name of that shape.
In make, the part of a file name that % matched in a pattern rule; available as $* in the recipe.
A rule make knows without being told, such as how to compile x.o from x.c. make -p lists them.
A make prerequisite written after |: it must exist first, but its being newer never makes the target rebuild. Used for output directories.
Several make targets written with &: that one recipe run produces together.
make's way of sharing a fixed number of parallel job slots (-j) between a make and the makes it starts.
Running make again from inside a recipe, typically once per folder with $(MAKE) -C dir, each with its own Makefile.

concepts.name: Rules: targets, prerequisites, recipes
concepts.summary: A Makefile is a list of rules: a target file, the files it's made from, and a tab-indented recipe of shell commands that makes it.
concepts.why: Every Makefile, from a two-line list of handy commands to the build of a large program, is made of this one construct.
concepts.body:
Many jobs turn some files into other files: a report made from data, a website made from text files, a program made from its code. **Make** automates such jobs. You describe once which file is made from which, and with what commands; then `make` runs only the steps that are needed. The description lives in a text file called a **Makefile**.

The classic use is building programs. A program written in a language such as C starts as **source code**: text files like `main.c`. A **compiler** (here the command `cc`) translates them into something the computer can run; that translating is called **compiling**.

Big programs are compiled in pieces. Each `.c` file becomes an **object file** (`.o`), a half-finished piece, and a final step, done by the **linker**, joins the pieces into one finished program. That's why the example below has three steps.

A Makefile is a list of **rules**, and a rule has three parts:

```
target: prerequisites
	recipe line
	recipe line
```

- The **target** is usually the file the rule produces, such as `app` or `main.o`.
- The **prerequisites** are the files (or other targets) it's made from.
- The **recipe** is one or more shell commands that make it. Each recipe line must start with a **tab character**, not spaces. Forgetting this gives the most famous make error: `*** missing separator.  Stop.`

Run `make target` to build one target, or plain `make` to build the **default goal**: the first target in the file (by convention called `all`).

To build a target, make first makes sure each prerequisite is up to date, using that prerequisite's own rule, and so on all the way down; only then does it run the target's recipe, if needed. So the rules form a tree of what's made from what, and make works through it from the bottom up.

make prints each recipe line before running it (you can switch that off, as shown later). If a command fails (non-zero exit status), make stops at once, so later steps never run on broken files. The file is normally called `Makefile` and sits in the project's top folder; `make -f other.mk` uses another file.
concepts.code:
# the finished program, linked from two object files
app: main.o util.o
	cc -o app main.o util.o

# compile main.c into main.o (util.h is a small file main.c uses)
main.o: main.c util.h
	cc -c main.c

util.o: util.c util.h
	cc -c util.c

# $ make
# cc -c main.c
# cc -c util.c
# cc -o app main.o util.o
# $ make
# make: 'app' is up to date.
takeaways: target: prerequisites, then tab-indented recipe lines
Plain make builds the first target in the file
make stops at the first failing command
pitfalls: Indenting recipes with spaces (often a text editor setting), which gives 'missing separator'.

quiz.q: What does make build when run with no arguments?
options: The first target in the Makefile
quiz.explain: The first target in the file is the default goal, unless the Makefile names another one.

concepts.name: How make decides what to rebuild
concepts.summary: make compares the times files were last changed: a target is rebuilt when it doesn't exist or any prerequisite is newer than it.
concepts.why: This rule is the whole point of make, and knowing it explains every 'why did/didn't it rebuild?' question.
concepts.body:
Every file records when it was last changed, its modification time: a **timestamp**, a recorded date and time. make's core rule is simple: a target is **out of date** if the file doesn't exist, or if any of its prerequisites was changed **more recently** than it. Out-of-date targets have their recipe run; up-to-date ones are skipped.

Because make applies this check all the way down the tree, editing one source file rebuilds exactly the chain above it: `util.c` changes, so `util.o` is rebuilt, which makes it newer than `app`, so `app` is linked again, while `main.o` is left alone.

Consequences you'll meet:

- A recipe must actually **create or update** the target file. If it doesn't, make thinks the target is missing every time and runs the recipe again.
- Listing every real input as a prerequisite matters. C files often pull in a **header file** (`.h`), a small shared file of declarations, with `#include`. If `main.c` includes `util.h` but the rule doesn't list it, editing the header won't trigger a rebuild, and you get **stale** results: old output that no longer matches the code.
- `touch file` updates a file's timestamp and forces everything made from it to rebuild; `make -B` rebuilds everything regardless.
- `make -n` (a dry run) prints what would be run without running it: the best way to check your rules.
- Timestamps can mislead: switching git branches, copying files while keeping their old times, or clocks that disagree between machines sharing files over a network can make make skip work it should do. When in doubt, run `make clean` (next lesson) and rebuild.
concepts.code:
out.txt: in.txt
	tr a-z A-Z < in.txt > out.txt

# $ echo hello > in.txt
# $ make            -> tr a-z A-Z < in.txt > out.txt
# $ make            -> make: 'out.txt' is up to date.
# $ touch in.txt    (in.txt is now newer than out.txt)
# $ make -n         -> tr a-z A-Z < in.txt > out.txt   (printed, not run)
# $ make            -> runs the recipe again
# $ make -B         -> rebuilds even if up to date
takeaways: A target is rebuilt if it is missing or older than any prerequisite
List every input, including headers, as a prerequisite
make -n shows what would run; make -B forces a rebuild
pitfalls: A recipe that never creates its target file, so it runs on every make.

quiz.q: app depends on a.o and b.o. You edit only b.c. What does a correct Makefile rebuild?
quiz.explain: b.o is now older than b.c, and the new b.o is newer than app, so both are rebuilt while a.o is left alone.

concepts.name: Phony targets and make as a task runner
concepts.summary: Declare targets that aren't files (all, clean, test) with .PHONY, and use a Makefile as a project's command menu.
concepts.why: Most Makefiles in modern projects are task runners, and .PHONY is what makes them reliable.
concepts.body:
Targets such as `clean`, `test` or `run` don't produce a file named after themselves. That works by accident, until someone creates a file or folder called `test`: make sees it exists with no prerequisites, decides it's up to date and silently does nothing.

Declare such targets **phony**:

```make
.PHONY: all clean test
```

A **phony target** is always considered out of date, so its recipe always runs, and make doesn't look for a file with that name.

Conventions worth following:

- `all` is the first target and builds everything; `clean` removes the files the build made; `test`, `lint` (check code style) and `install` do what they say.
- A phony target can depend on other targets: `check: lint test` runs both.
- Use `rm -f` in `clean` so it doesn't fail when the files are already gone.

Many projects use make as a **task runner**: a menu of the project's common commands. Every project then starts the same way (`make test`, `make run`), make takes care of tasks that need other tasks first, and it's installed almost everywhere. A self-documenting `help` target is a common touch: put `## description` after each target and print them with a little grep and awk.

Set `.DEFAULT_GOAL := help` if you'd rather show help than build when someone types just `make`.
concepts.code:
.PHONY: help test lint check clean
.DEFAULT_GOAL := help

help:  ## show this help
	@grep -E '^[a-z]+:.*## ' $(MAKEFILE_LIST) | awk -F':.*## ' '{printf "%-8s %s\n", $$1, $$2}'

test:  ## run the tests
	python3 -m pytest -q

lint:  ## check code style
	ruff check .

check: lint test  ## lint, then test

clean:  ## remove build output
	rm -rf build dist .pytest_cache

# $ make
# help     show this help
# test     run the tests
# ...
takeaways: Mark targets that aren't files with .PHONY so they always run
Conventional targets: all, clean, test, install
A phony target can just depend on others, like `check: lint test`
pitfalls: Forgetting .PHONY, so a folder named test or build makes the target silently do nothing.

quiz.q: A project has a folder called docs and a rule docs: with no .PHONY. What does make docs do?
options: Reports docs is up to date and runs nothing
quiz.explain: docs exists and has no prerequisites newer than it, so make considers the target up to date.

concepts.name: Variables: =, :=, ?= and +=
concepts.summary: Define and use variables with $(NAME), and know the four ways to set them: =, :=, ?= and +=.
concepts.why: Variables keep the compiler's name, its options and file lists in one place, and let people change them when they run make.
concepts.body:
Make variables hold text, like bash variables. Define them near the top of the Makefile and use them as `$(NAME)` (or `${NAME}`). Some names are conventional: `CC` and `CXX` (the C and C++ compilers), `CFLAGS` and `CXXFLAGS` (options for them), and `CPPFLAGS`, `LDFLAGS` and `LDLIBS` (more compiler and linker options).

There are four ways to assign a value:

- `=` makes a **recursively expanded variable**: the value is stored as written, and any `$(...)` inside it is filled in **every time** the variable is used, so later changes to those variables show up.
- `:=` (or `::=`) makes a **simply expanded variable**: the right-hand side is filled in **once**, right away. Predictable and cheaper; prefer it for values that are computed.
- `?=` sets the variable only if it has no value yet: a way to give a default that an environment variable can replace.
- `+=` adds more text to the end, with a space in between.

Values can come from three places, from weakest to strongest: environment variables, the Makefile, and the `make` command you type. `make CFLAGS=-O0` replaces the Makefile's value completely (unless the Makefile marks it with the word `override`).

A dollar sign in a Makefile always starts a make variable, so `$HOME` means `$(H)` followed by `OME`. Write `$(HOME)` to read the environment variable through make, or `$$HOME` to hand the text `$HOME` on to the shell. Single-letter variables like `$@` (next lessons) don't need parentheses.

Spaces matter: spaces at the end of a value are kept, which can break paths.
concepts.code:
PREFIX  ?= /usr/local          # default, unless already set
CFLAGS  := -Wall -O2
CFLAGS  += -g                  # now: -Wall -O2 -g
SRC     := main.c util.c

A = $(B)                       # filled in when A is used
B = later
X := $(Y)                      # filled in now: Y is still empty
Y = later

show:
	@echo "PREFIX=$(PREFIX) CFLAGS=$(CFLAGS)"
	@echo "A=$(A) X=$(X)"
	@echo "home via make: $(HOME), via shell: $$HOME"

# $ make show
# PREFIX=/usr/local CFLAGS=-Wall -O2 -g
# A=later X=
# $ make show CFLAGS=-O0
# PREFIX=/usr/local CFLAGS=-O0
# $ PREFIX=/opt make show
# PREFIX=/opt CFLAGS=-Wall -O2 -g
takeaways: = fills in values each time it's used, := once when defined
?= sets a default, += appends
Assignments on the make command win over the Makefile; write $$ for a $ meant for the shell
pitfalls: Writing $HOME or $PATH in a recipe; make reads it as $(H)OME. Use $$HOME.
Writing CC ?= gcc: make already sets CC to cc, so the default never applies. Use CC := gcc or let users pass CC=.

quiz.q: Given X := $(Y) followed by Y = 1, what is $(X)?
quiz.explain: := fills in the value immediately, and Y had no value yet at that point.

quiz.q: Which assignment lets an environment variable PREFIX take precedence?
quiz.explain: ?= only assigns when the variable has no value yet, and a value from the environment counts.

concepts.name: Automatic variables: $@, $<, $^
concepts.summary: Write recipes once using automatic variables: $@ the target, $< the first prerequisite, $^ all prerequisites, $? the newer ones.
concepts.why: They remove repetition from recipes and are essential for the rules with `%` that every real Makefile uses (next lesson).
concepts.body:
Inside a recipe, make sets **automatic variables** describing the rule being run:

- `$@` the target's file name.
- `$<` the first prerequisite.
- `$^` all prerequisites, without duplicates (`$+` keeps them, sometimes needed when the linker cares about order).
- `$?` the prerequisites that are newer than the target.
- `$*` the stem: the part matched by `%` in a rule written with `%` (next lesson).
- `$(@D)` and `$(@F)` the **directory** (folder) part and the file-name part of `$@`.

So a link rule becomes `$(CC) $(LDFLAGS) -o $@ $^ $(LDLIBS)`, the same text whatever the target is called.

A common habit is creating the output directory in the recipe: `@mkdir -p $(@D)` before writing into `build/obj/x.o`.

Automatic variables only have values **inside recipes**. Using `$@` in a prerequisite list, or in a variable defined outside a recipe, doesn't work (one rarely used make feature, secondary expansion, is the only way around this).

The order of prerequisites matters for `$<`: put the main source file first and headers after it, so `$<` is the `.c` file you want to compile.
concepts.code:
CC     := cc
CFLAGS := -Wall -O2

build/app: build/main.o build/util.o
	$(CC) -o $@ $^

build/main.o: main.c util.h
	@mkdir -p $(@D)
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c $< -o $@

build/util.o: util.c util.h
	@mkdir -p $(@D)
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c $< -o $@

# $ make
# cc -Wall -O2 -c main.c -o build/main.o
# cc -Wall -O2 -c util.c -o build/util.o
# cc -o build/app build/main.o build/util.o
takeaways: $@ target, $< first prerequisite, $^ all prerequisites
$(@D) is the target's directory: mkdir -p $(@D) before writing
Automatic variables only exist inside recipes
pitfalls: Listing a header before the .c file, so $< passes the header to the compiler.

quiz.q: In the rule lib.a: x.o y.o z.o, after only y.o changed, what is $? in the recipe?
quiz.explain: $? lists only the prerequisites newer than the target.

concepts.name: Pattern rules and built-in rules
concepts.summary: Write one rule for many files with % patterns like %.o: %.c, and know make's built-in implicit rules and how to turn them off.
concepts.why: Pattern rules are how a Makefile scales from two files to two hundred without growing.
concepts.body:
A **pattern rule** uses `%` to match any non-empty part of a name, called the **stem**:

```make
build/%.o: src/%.c
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c $< -o $@
```

To build `build/net.o`, make matches the stem `net`, looks for `src/net.c` and runs the recipe with `$@` and `$<` filled in. One rule now covers every source file.

Combine it with variables listing the object files, usually computed from the list of source files:

```make
SRC := $(wildcard src/*.c)
OBJ := $(SRC:src/%.c=build/%.o)
```

make also has **built-in implicit rules**. It already knows how to make `x.o` from `x.c` with `$(CC) $(CPPFLAGS) $(CFLAGS) -c`, and how to link `x` from `x.o`. That's why a Makefile containing only `app: app.o` can work. `make -p` prints all of them.

Built-in rules are convenient for tiny projects but surprising in bigger ones, and they slow make down by trying many possible rules. Many projects switch them off with `MAKEFLAGS += --no-builtin-rules` and an empty `.SUFFIXES:` line, and write their own pattern rules instead.

**Static pattern rules** limit a pattern to a given list of targets: `$(OBJ): build/%.o: src/%.c`. They're more explicit, and fail loudly when a source file is missing.
concepts.code:
CC     := cc
CFLAGS := -Wall -O2
SRC    := $(wildcard src/*.c)
OBJ    := $(SRC:src/%.c=build/%.o)

MAKEFLAGS += --no-builtin-rules
.SUFFIXES:

build/app: $(OBJ)
	$(CC) -o $@ $^

build/%.o: src/%.c
	@mkdir -p $(@D)
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c $< -o $@

.PHONY: clean
clean:
	rm -rf build

# with src/main.c and src/util.c:
# $ make
# cc -Wall -O2 -c src/main.c -o build/main.o
# cc -Wall -O2 -c src/util.c -o build/util.o
# cc -o build/app build/main.o build/util.o
takeaways: %.o: %.c matches any stem; $< and $@ fill in the names
Derive object file lists from source lists with $(SRC:src/%.c=build/%.o)
make has built-in rules; --no-builtin-rules makes builds explicit
pitfalls: A pattern rule silently not applying because the prerequisite path is wrong; make then reports 'No rule to make target'.

quiz.q: With the rule out/%.html: pages/%.md, what is the stem when building out/about.html?
quiz.explain: % matched the part between the fixed beginning out/ and the fixed ending .html.

concepts.name: Text functions: wildcard, patsubst, foreach
concepts.summary: Compute file lists and options with make's text functions: wildcard, patsubst, subst, filter, addprefix, notdir, foreach and shell.
concepts.why: Functions let a Makefile discover files and transform names instead of hard-coding every path.
concepts.body:
Make has built-in **functions**: named operations that take some text and give back new text. A call looks like `$(name arg1,arg2)`. Note there's no space after the commas, unless you want one in the result. The most useful:

- `$(wildcard src/*.c)` the files matching a pattern (only ones that exist right now).
- `$(patsubst %.c,%.o,$(SRC))` replaces by pattern; the shorthand `$(SRC:.c=.o)` does the same for endings.
- `$(subst from,to,text)` simple text replacement.
- `$(filter %.c,$(FILES))` keeps matching words; `filter-out` drops them.
- `$(addprefix build/,$(OBJ))`, `$(addsuffix ...)`, `$(notdir ...)`, `$(dir ...)`, `$(basename ...)`.
- `$(sort list)` sorts and **removes duplicates**; `$(words ...)`, `$(word n,...)`, `$(firstword ...)`.
- `$(foreach v,list,text)` repeats text for each word.
- `$(shell cmd)` runs a shell command and inserts its output (its lines joined with spaces).
- `$(if cond,then,else)`, `$(error msg)`, `$(warning msg)`, `$(info msg)` for checks, and for printing values while you fix a Makefile.

make thinks in **words separated by spaces**, so file names containing spaces are effectively unsupported. Keep build paths free of spaces.

Assign function results with `:=` so they're worked out once. With `=`, a `$(shell ...)` call would run again every time the variable is used.
concepts.code:
SRC   := $(wildcard src/*.c)
OBJ   := $(patsubst src/%.c,build/%.o,$(SRC))
NAMES := $(notdir $(basename $(SRC)))
TESTS := $(filter test_%,$(NAMES))
DIRS  := $(sort $(dir $(OBJ)) build/ build/)
GIT   := $(shell git rev-parse --short HEAD 2>/dev/null || echo none)

ifeq ($(SRC),)
$(error no sources found in src/)
endif

show:
	@echo SRC=$(SRC)
	@echo OBJ=$(OBJ)
	@echo NAMES=$(NAMES) TESTS=$(TESTS)
	@echo DIRS=$(DIRS) GIT=$(GIT)
	@echo $(foreach n,$(NAMES),bin/$(n))

# with src/main.c, src/util.c, src/test_util.c:
# SRC=src/main.c src/test_util.c src/util.c
# OBJ=build/main.o build/test_util.o build/util.o
# NAMES=main test_util util TESTS=test_util
# DIRS=build/ GIT=none
# bin/main bin/test_util bin/util
takeaways: $(wildcard), $(patsubst) and $(SRC:.c=.o) build file lists
filter, addprefix, notdir, sort and foreach transform word lists
Assign $(shell ...) with := so it runs once
pitfalls: Adding a space after a comma, as in $(subst a, b,x), which puts the space into the result.

quiz.explain: Words that don't match the pattern are passed through unchanged.

concepts.name: How recipes run in the shell
concepts.summary: Each recipe line runs in its own shell; learn @, -, line continuations, $$, .ONESHELL, SHELL and .DELETE_ON_ERROR.
concepts.why: Most confusing Makefile problems are really about how recipe lines are handed to the shell.
concepts.body:
make hands each recipe line to a **separate** shell (`/bin/sh -c 'line'`). So nothing carries over between lines: a `cd dir` on one line has no effect on the next, and neither does setting a shell variable. Join commands that belong together on one line with `&&`, or continue a line with a backslash at its end.

Line prefixes:

- `@` don't print the command before running it.
- `-` ignore a failure of this command and keep going.
- `+` run even under `make -n` (used when a recipe starts make again).

Shell code and make code mix in recipes. make fills in `$(VAR)` first, and the shell then sees the result. So the shell's own variables, and its `$(command)` form (which runs a command and uses its output), need **doubled dollars**: `$$f`, `$$(date)`.

Useful settings:

- `SHELL := /bin/bash` and `.SHELLFLAGS := -eu -o pipefail -c` run recipes in bash, stopping at the first error, unset variable or failed pipeline part.
- `.ONESHELL:` runs the whole recipe in one shell, so `cd` and variables carry over (only the first line's `@` and `-` apply).
- `.DELETE_ON_ERROR:` deletes a target whose recipe failed. Without it, a half-written output file is newer than its inputs, and the next `make` happily treats it as up to date.

Recipe lines run one after another and stop at the first non-zero exit status, unless the line starts with `-`.
concepts.code:
SHELL := /bin/bash
.SHELLFLAGS := -eu -o pipefail -c
.DELETE_ON_ERROR:

wrong:
	cd /tmp
	pwd                       # still the project folder!

right:
	cd /tmp && pwd            # /tmp

loop:
	@for f in a b c; do \
	  echo "item $$f"; \
	done                      # item a / item b / item c

tolerant:
	-rm nonexistent-file      # error printed, but make continues
	@echo "stamp: $$(date +%F)"

report.txt: data.txt
	grep -c ok data.txt | tee $@    # if grep fails, report.txt is deleted
takeaways: Every recipe line runs in a new shell: use && or backslashes to join
@ silences, - ignores errors; $$ hands a $ on to the shell
.DELETE_ON_ERROR removes half-written targets after a failure
pitfalls: Splitting cd build and make on two lines, so the second command runs in the wrong folder.

quiz.q: A recipe has two lines: export X=1, then echo $$X. What is printed?
quiz.explain: Each line runs in a separate shell, so the export from the first line is gone in the second.

concepts.name: Automatic header dependencies
concepts.summary: Let the compiler write the list of headers each file uses (-MMD -MP) and include it, so editing a header rebuilds exactly the right object files.
concepts.why: Hand-kept header lists always go wrong eventually; generated lists keep builds that only redo what changed correct.
concepts.body:
An object file depends on its source file **and every header it includes**, plus the headers those headers include, and so on. Listing them by hand doesn't scale and quietly goes out of date. Compilers can write the list for you while compiling:

- `-MMD` writes a `.d` file next to the object file (for example `build/main.d`) containing a make rule `build/main.o: src/main.c src/util.h ...`, leaving out the system's own headers.
- `-MP` adds an empty phony rule for each header, so deleting or renaming a header doesn't break the build with "No rule to make target".

Then include the generated files at the end of the Makefile:

```make
-include $(OBJ:.o=.d)
```

The leading `-` ignores missing files: on the first build there are no `.d` files yet, and that's fine, because every object file has to be compiled anyway. After that, each compile refreshes its `.d` file, so the lists stay correct as the includes change.

This works with GCC and Clang (`-MMD -MP`); Microsoft's compiler has `/showIncludes` instead, one reason C++ projects that must build on several **operating systems** (Windows, macOS, Linux) tend to use CMake. The same idea works elsewhere: many tools can write such a list (`sass`, `go list -deps`) for a Makefile to include.

Add `CPPFLAGS += -MMD -MP` so the options are part of the standard compile rule.
concepts.code:
CC       := cc
CPPFLAGS := -MMD -MP -Isrc
CFLAGS   := -Wall -O2
SRC      := $(wildcard src/*.c)
OBJ      := $(SRC:src/%.c=build/%.o)

build/app: $(OBJ)
	$(CC) -o $@ $^

build/%.o: src/%.c
	@mkdir -p $(@D)
	$(CC) $(CPPFLAGS) $(CFLAGS) -c $< -o $@

-include $(OBJ:.o=.d)

# build/main.d, written by the compiler:
#   build/main.o: src/main.c src/util.h
#   src/util.h:
# $ touch src/util.h && make
#   recompiles main.o and util.o (both include util.h), then relinks
takeaways: -MMD -MP make the compiler write .d files listing each file's headers
-include $(OBJ:.o=.d) pulls them in and ignores missing ones
Headers, and the headers they include, are then tracked automatically
pitfalls: Omitting -MP, so deleting a header breaks the build until the .d files are removed.

quiz.q: Why is -include used instead of include for the .d files?
options: -include runs the files as shell scripts
The .d files don't exist before the first build, and that shouldn't be an error
quiz.explain: The dash makes missing files harmless; on a clean build every object file is compiled anyway.

concepts.name: Parallel builds with -j
concepts.summary: Run independent recipes at the same time with make -j, fix the missing prerequisites this exposes, and use order-only prerequisites.
concepts.why: Running recipes side by side divides build time by the number of CPU cores, but only if every rule lists everything it needs.
concepts.body:
`make -j8` runs up to eight recipes at the same time; `make -j$(nproc)` uses every **CPU core** (the parts of the computer's main chip that can each run one thing at a time; `nproc` prints how many there are). make only starts a target once all its prerequisites are done, so if every rule lists everything it needs, running recipes side by side is automatically safe.

Builds with `-j` **expose missing prerequisites**. If `app` needs `gen/config.h` but its rule doesn't say so, a one-at-a-time build may work by luck of ordering, while `-j` builds fail at random. Fix the rules rather than adding `.NOTPARALLEL`.

Tools for precise rules:

- **Order-only prerequisites**, after a `|`: `build/%.o: src/%.c | build` means "build must exist first, but its timestamp doesn't matter". Perfect for output directories, whose timestamps change whenever a file is added to them.
- A **grouped target**, `a.c a.h &: spec.y` (GNU make 4.3+), says one recipe produces several files together. A plain `a.c a.h: spec.y` means two separate rules, and under `-j` the command that writes them may run twice at once.
- `--output-sync=target` (`-O`) holds back each target's output until it's finished, so messages from recipes running side by side don't get mixed up.

When a recipe starts make again in another folder, use `$(MAKE)`: then all of them share one pool of job slots (the **jobserver**) instead of each starting its own eight. `MAKEFLAGS += -j8` inside the Makefile is possible but surprises users; usually leave `-j` to whoever runs make.
concepts.code:
SRC := $(wildcard src/*.c)
OBJ := $(SRC:src/%.c=build/%.o)

build/app: $(OBJ)
	cc -o $@ $^

# order-only: the directory must exist, its timestamp is ignored
build/%.o: src/%.c gen/version.h | build
	cc -Igen -c $< -o $@

build:
	mkdir -p $@

# grouped target: one run of the generator produces both files
gen/version.h gen/version.c &: version.txt
	@mkdir -p gen
	./mkversion.sh version.txt gen/version.h gen/version.c

# $ make -j"$(nproc)" -O
takeaways: make -jN runs independent recipes at the same time
Random -j failures mean a rule is missing a prerequisite
Use | for order-only prerequisites (directories) and &: for grouped targets
pitfalls: Making object files depend normally on their output directory, so every new file in it triggers rebuilds.

quiz.q: Why put an output directory after | in a prerequisite list?
options: Because directories can't be normal prerequisites
So it must exist first but its changing timestamp never forces rebuilds
To delete it after the build
quiz.explain: Order-only prerequisites only set the order; they don't count when make checks what's out of date.

concepts.name: Conditionals, includes and configuration
concepts.summary: Adapt a Makefile with ifeq/ifdef, split it with include, and support build modes like `DEBUG=1` and settings per operating system.
concepts.why: Real builds need a mode for finding problems and a fast release mode, differences between operating systems, and shared pieces without copy-paste.
concepts.body:
**Conditionals** (`ifeq`, `ifdef` and friends, which keep or skip lines depending on a test) are checked when make reads the Makefile, not when recipes run:

```make
ifeq ($(DEBUG),1)
  CFLAGS += -O0 -g
else
  CFLAGS += -O2
endif
```

Also available: `ifneq`, `ifdef VAR` (true if the variable has a non-empty value), `ifndef`. Detect the **operating system** (Windows, macOS or Linux) with `UNAME_S := $(shell uname -s)` and `ifeq ($(UNAME_S),Darwin)` (Darwin means macOS); on Windows `$(OS)` is `Windows_NT`.

Don't indent these lines with a tab: lines beginning with a tab are treated as recipe lines.

**include** reads other makefiles as if they were pasted in: `include config.mk` for shared settings, `-include local.mk` for optional settings each developer keeps for themselves (not committed to git). make also tries to **remake** included files: if there's a rule for `config.mk`, make builds it, then starts reading again. That allows generated settings files, but can surprise you.

For build modes that shouldn't mix, put outputs in separate **directories** (folders), such as `build/debug` and `build/release`. Then switching `DEBUG=1` doesn't leave you linking object files compiled with different options. make doesn't notice option changes on its own; a common trick is a `build/flags.txt` file that is rewritten only when the options change, listed as a prerequisite.

`$(MAKECMDGOALS)` holds the targets you typed after `make`, handy to skip slow includes when only `clean` was asked for.
concepts.code:
UNAME_S := $(shell uname -s)
MODE    := $(if $(filter 1,$(DEBUG)),debug,release)
BUILD   := build/$(MODE)

ifeq ($(MODE),debug)
  CFLAGS += -O0 -g -fsanitize=address
else
  CFLAGS += -O2 -DNDEBUG
endif

ifeq ($(UNAME_S),Darwin)
  LDLIBS += -framework CoreFoundation
endif

-include local.mk          # optional, not in git

info:
	@echo "$(MODE) -> $(BUILD), CFLAGS=$(CFLAGS)"

# $ make info            -> release -> build/release, CFLAGS=-O2 -DNDEBUG
# $ make info DEBUG=1    -> debug -> build/debug, CFLAGS=-O0 -g -fsanitize=address
takeaways: ifeq/ifdef are evaluated while reading the Makefile
include shares fragments; -include makes them optional
Separate output directories per build mode
pitfalls: Indenting ifeq with a tab among rules, so make treats it as a shell command.

options: When make reads the Makefile, before building anything
Only when the target named DEBUG is built
quiz.explain: Conditionals are checked while make reads the file; they decide which lines become part of the Makefile.

concepts.name: Two phases: reading and running
concepts.summary: Understand make's read phase and build phase, immediate versus deferred expansion, and how $(eval) and $(call) generate rules.
concepts.why: This model explains every puzzling variable value and unlocks generating rules programmatically.
concepts.body:
GNU make works in **two phases**. In the **read phase** it reads all makefiles, works out what each line means (it **parses** them), fills in whatever must be known right away, and builds its map of which target needs which, the **dependency graph**. In the **build phase** it decides what's out of date and runs recipes.

Each construct is filled in either **immediately** (during reading) or **deferred** (later, when it's used):

- Immediate: the right side of `:=`, `::=` and `!=`, the targets and prerequisites of rules, and conditionals.
- Deferred: the right side of `=` and `?=`, `define` blocks, and **recipes**, which are filled in only just before they run. `+=` keeps the kind the variable already had.

That's why a recipe can use a variable defined further down the file, while a prerequisite list can't.

`$(call fn,a,b)` fills in a variable with `$(1)`, `$(2)` set to the arguments: your own functions. `$(eval text)` takes text and reads it as **Makefile code** during the read phase, so you can generate rules in a loop:

```make
$(foreach p,$(PROGRAMS),$(eval $(call PROGRAM_template,$(p))))
```

Here `PROGRAM_template` is a **template**: a variable holding the text of a rule, with blanks for `call` to fill in. Inside it, anything that must survive until `eval` reads it needs `$$`: one level of `$` is used up by `call`, the second by `eval`. To check a template, replace `$(eval ...)` with `$(info ...)` to print the generated text.
concepts.code:
PROGRAMS := server client
server_SRC := server.c net.c
client_SRC := client.c net.c

define PROGRAM_template
$(1): $$($(1)_SRC:.c=.o)
	$$(CC) -o $$@ $$^
ALL += $(1)
endef

$(foreach p,$(PROGRAMS),$(eval $(call PROGRAM_template,$(p))))

all: $(ALL)

show:
	@echo "ALL=$(ALL)"
	@echo "late=$(LATE)"

# recipes are expanded later, so a variable defined below the rule works
LATE = defined after the rule

# $(info $(call PROGRAM_template,server)) would print:
#   server: $(server_SRC:.c=.o)
#   	$(CC) -o $@ $^
#   ALL += server
takeaways: The read phase builds the graph; the build phase runs recipes
:= is immediate, = and ?= are deferred, recipes are filled in just before running
$(eval $(call template,...)) generates rules; protect $ with $$
pitfalls: Using a variable in a prerequisite list before it is defined in the file; prerequisites are expanded immediately.

quiz.q: Why can a recipe use a variable that is only assigned near the end of the Makefile?
options: Recipes are expanded only when they are about to run, after all makefiles are read
It can't; this is an error
quiz.explain: Recipes are filled in during the build phase, by which time the whole file has been read.

concepts.name: Recursive versus non-recursive make
concepts.summary: Why running make separately in each folder hides what depends on what and slows builds, and how one non-recursive Makefile with includes fixes it.
concepts.why: Large Makefile-based projects live or die by this design choice.
concepts.body:
A common layout has a top-level Makefile that runs `$(MAKE) -C lib` and `$(MAKE) -C app`, each folder with its own Makefile. This is **recursive make**. It's simple, but it has well-known problems, described in Peter Miller's paper "Recursive Make Considered Harmful":

- Each sub-make sees only **part of the dependency graph**. If `app` needs a header generated in `lib`, the top level must order the sub-makes by hand, and getting it wrong gives stale or broken builds.
- Running several recipes at once suffers: sub-makes run one folder after another, and each one rereads and rechecks its files.
- Even when nothing changed, every sub-make still runs.

The **non-recursive** alternative: one make process, one complete graph. Each folder contributes a fragment (`lib/module.mk`) that adds to shared variables and defines rules with paths starting from the top folder, and the top-level Makefile includes them all. make then knows every link between targets, runs recipes from different folders at the same time, and does nothing when nothing changed.

If you do use recursive make (say, for other people's projects bundled into yours, with their own Makefiles), always call `$(MAKE)`, not `make`: it passes on options such as `-j` and `-n` and joins the jobserver. Variables reach sub-makes only if exported (`export CFLAGS`) or passed in the make command.

At large scale, tools like CMake (which writes Ninja build files) or Meson usually replace hand-written Makefiles altogether.
concepts.code:
# top-level Makefile: one make, one complete graph
CFLAGS  := -Wall -O2 -Iinclude
OBJ     :=
PROGS   :=
# the fragments define targets first, so name the default goal
.DEFAULT_GOAL := all

include lib/module.mk
include app/module.mk

all: $(PROGS)

%.o: %.c
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c $< -o $@

# ---- lib/module.mk ----
# LIB_OBJ := lib/strings.o lib/hash.o
# OBJ += $(LIB_OBJ)
# lib/libcore.a: $(LIB_OBJ)
# 	$(AR) rcs $@ $^

# ---- app/module.mk ----
# PROGS += app/app
# app/app: app/main.o lib/libcore.a
# 	$(CC) -o $@ $^
takeaways: Recursive make splits the dependency graph into pieces that can't see each other
Non-recursive: include per-folder fragments into one Makefile
If you must use recursive make, call $(MAKE) so options and the jobserver are passed on
pitfalls: Calling plain make in a recipe, which ignores -j limits and -n dry runs.

quiz.q: What is the main correctness problem with recursive make?
options: No single make process sees the whole dependency graph
quiz.explain: Links between folders are invisible to each sub-make, so the order must be kept right by hand.

concepts.name: Debugging Makefiles
concepts.summary: Find out why make did or didn't rebuild something with -n, --trace, --debug, -p and $(info), and understand its common error messages.
concepts.why: Make's terse errors are easy once you know how to ask it what it's thinking.
concepts.body:
When a build does something unexpected, ask make directly:

- `make -n` prints the commands it would run, without running them.
- `make --trace` (4.0+) prints each recipe with the reason it ran, for example "target 'build/x.o' does not exist" or "prerequisite 'src/x.c' is newer than target".
- `make --debug=b` (basic) or `--debug=v` (verbose) explains its decisions; `--debug=i` adds the search for implicit rules, the answer to "why was that weird built-in rule used?".
- `make -p` prints everything make knows after reading: every variable with where it came from, and every rule. Add `-q` or a target that doesn't exist to avoid building: `make -pq | less`.
- `$(info VAR=$(VAR))` and `$(warning ...)` print during the read phase; `$(error ...)` stops.
- `make -B -n target` shows the complete chain of recipes for a target.

Common messages decoded:

- `missing separator`: a recipe line not indented with a tab, or a stray line of text.
- `No rule to make target 'X', needed by 'Y'`: a prerequisite doesn't exist and no rule (written out or pattern) can create it; often a typo, a deleted header still listed in a `.d` file, or a pattern rule whose source path doesn't match.
- `Circular X <- Y dependency dropped`: the graph has a loop.
- `target 'X' given more than once in the same rule` or `overriding recipe`: two recipes for one target, usually a copy-paste mistake.

`$(origin VAR)` and `$(flavor VAR)` tell you where a variable came from and whether it's a recursively expanded or simply expanded variable.
concepts.code:
# Makefile with a mistake: header path is wrong
build/app.o: src/app.c src/app.hh
	cc -c $< -o $@

$(info CC is '$(CC)' from $(origin CC), flavor $(flavor CC))

# $ make build/app.o
# CC is 'cc' from default, flavor recursive
# make: *** No rule to make target 'src/app.hh', needed by 'build/app.o'.  Stop.

# after fixing it:
# $ touch src/app.c && make --trace build/app.o
# Makefile:3: update target 'build/app.o' due to: src/app.c
# cc -c src/app.c -o build/app.o

# $ make -p -f /dev/null | grep -A2 '^%.o: %.c'
# %.o: %.c
# #  recipe to execute (built-in):
# 	$(COMPILE.c) $(OUTPUT_OPTION) $<
takeaways: --trace says why each recipe ran; -n shows what would run
-p dumps all variables and rules, including built-ins
'No rule to make target' means a missing file with no rule to create it
pitfalls: Guessing at rebuild problems instead of running make --trace or --debug=b, which states the reason.

quiz.q: make reports: No rule to make target 'util.h', needed by 'main.o'. What is the most likely cause?
options: util.h doesn't exist (renamed or deleted) but is still listed, perhaps in a stale .d file
The recipe for main.o uses spaces
quiz.explain: make can't find the file and has no rule to create it, so the prerequisite list is out of date.
